the short movement before an attack lands
a system that keeps the camera and attacks aimed at one enemy
the invisible area the game uses to decide if an attack connects

the game fights for you, while you choose the team, timing and upgrades

lessons.title: Combat has three verbs: hit, move, guard

cards.text: A military thinker said every fighting action is one of three things: **hitting, moving or guarding.** Design all three, not just attacks.

Violence is popular in games because it's the fastest loop of action, result and reward: press, enemy reacts, reward. How violent you make it (who does it, how often, how graphic) decides your age rating.
Clash Royale, Brawl Stars and Squad Busters use cartoon violence: enemies pop and vanish instead of bleeding. That keeps ratings low and widens the audience.
The "tap, enemy pops, coins fly" loop is the F2P core loop in miniature. Survivor.io runs it dozens of times a second. Non-violent conflict is huge too: match-3 levels are battles against a board.
H-M-G: Hit, Move, Guard.

check.q: What are the three elements of combat?
options: Hit, move and guard
Attack, reward and level up
Aim, shoot and reload
check.why: Every fighting action falls into hitting, moving or guarding.

cards.text: Combat style should express **who the character is**, and **the weapon decides how they fight.**
A sneaky character fights from shadows with quick strikes. A brute swings slow, heavy blows. A signature weapon, like a giant sword or a whip, shapes every move.
Cloud's huge sword in Final Fantasy VII defines his whole fighting style. Without it, he'd just be a guy with spiky hair.
In hero-collecting games, each hero's weapon and personality must read instantly in their attack: a Brawl Stars brawler's shot shape tells you their role before you read any stats.
Show me your weapon and I'll tell you who you are.

check.q: What should shape a character's fighting style?
options: Their personality and signature weapon
Whatever animation is cheapest to make
The fighting style of the enemies
check.why: Combat is character. The weapon and personality decide how they fight.

lessons.title: Ranges, heights and the attack matrix

cards.text: The right attack depends on **how far away and how high** the target is. Spread attacks across ranges and heights, and track them all in an **attack matrix.**

- **Ranges:** close (punches), medium (sword swings), long (projectiles), area (hits everything around).
- **Heights:** standing, low, high (jump attacks), aerial.
- **Directions:** vertical and horizontal swings.
An attack matrix is a table of every move: range, damage, speed, height, special effect. If two moves have the same row, one of them isn't needed.
In Clash Royale, ranges and heights became card roles: air vs ground, splash vs single target, cards that only hit buildings. The attack matrix turned into the whole strategy.
If two moves have the same profile, one gets cut.

check.q: What does an attack matrix help you guarantee?
options: Every attack is different and useful
Every attack does the same damage
Fewer animations
check.why: Comparing moves side by side shows overlaps so each move earns its place.

cards.text: **Timing** is one of the biggest keys to great combat. Inputs should feel instant. And **a hit must look, sound and feel like a hit**: the feedback is the reward.
Quick attacks chain into a rhythm. Slow wind-ups are only for heavy, risky attacks with a huge payoff. On every hit, the enemy flinches, sparks fly, the sound punches and the screen shakes slightly.
Watch out for the "moonwalking hero" who swings three times at empty air because nobody made him step forward. Small attacks should move the character toward the enemy.
On phones, add a tiny vibration on big hits, and make sure the hit reads without sound, since many players play muted.
Quick, quick, SLAM. And a hit with no reaction is a high-five to a ghost.

check.q: When is a slow wind-up attack okay?
options: When it's risky but has a big payoff
For every basic attack in the game
Never: slow attacks always feel bad
check.why: Slow attacks are a bet. They need a reward worth the risk.

cards.text: People want games that **make them look cool.** Finishers, lock-on and smart targeting turn normal players into action heroes. Use them carefully.

- **Lock-on** keeps the player aimed at one enemy, so anyone looks like an expert.
- **Finishing moves** end a fight in style.
- **Weapon upgrades** should be visible: a sword that glows or burns, not just "+3".
- **Special kills** like stealth takedowns need strict conditions.
In the Batman Arkham games, Batman almost never misses. The game helps the player chain attacks, and everyone feels like Batman.
Auto-aim in Brawl Stars and auto-attack in Archero are mobile lock-on. Upgrades should change how the weapon looks, because players can't see numbers.
+3 is invisible. Flames are forever.

check.q: How should a weapon upgrade be shown?
options: Visibly: it glows or changes look
Only as a number in a menu
Not at all, to keep it subtle
check.why: Players feel upgrades they can see, not hidden numbers.

lessons.title: Missing is fine, but help the strugglers

cards.text: Letting players miss builds **mastery**: improving feels earned. But players who keep failing should get **quiet help**, because the real goal is to keep them playing.
If a player keeps missing, the game can quietly make hitboxes a bit bigger or enemies a bit slower, without saying so.
In F2P, quiet help after several losses (a slightly easier board, a free booster) keeps players from quitting. Never do the opposite: secretly harder games for players likely to pay.
Secretly widen the doorway.

check.q: A player keeps failing the same fight. What's a good response?
options: Quietly give a bit of help
Make the fight even harder
Show an ad before each retry
check.why: Hidden assistance keeps strugglers playing without embarrassing them.

lessons.title: Moving: the goal is not to get hit

cards.text: In any martial art, **moving matters as much as attacking.** The goal of a real fight is not to get hit. Give players moves that escape damage, and moves that combine with attacks.

- **Dodge:** gets you clear of danger.
- **Dash:** gets you there fast, and can hurt on the way.
- **Jump attack:** hits from above.
Make sure a dodge actually clears an enemy's attack. A dodge one step too short is worse than none.
Give hitboxes a little extra room, like comfortable trousers. A dodge that "should have" worked but didn't feels unfair.
In survivor-like games, movement is the whole skill: you dodge and position while attacks fire automatically. Give mobile dodges a generous window, because touch is less precise.
Dodge clears, dash hurts, stomp bounces.

check.q: What's the real goal of a fight, according to martial arts?
options: Not getting hit
Hitting as often as possible
Using every weapon
check.why: Movement and avoiding damage matter as much as attacking.

cards.text: **Blocks must be instant.** How long a shield lasts decides whether players use it. Armour can protect, inform, unlock abilities and let players customise their look.
If a shield breaks too easily, players are scared to use it and never block. If it never breaks, fights become boring. Find the middle.
In World of Warcraft, a cool helmet works like a walking billboard: other players see it and think "I could have that too".
Armour and gear that change your look are perfect for F2P: they show progress, create "me too" desire in other players, and can be sold as cosmetics without changing who wins.
A shield you're scared to break is a shield you'll never use.

check.q: What happens if a shield breaks too easily?
options: Players avoid using it
Players use it more
Fights become easier
check.why: If blocking feels risky, players stop blocking.

lessons.title: Shooting is rhythm: the Three As

cards.text: "Aim and pull the trigger" hides a big design space. Ranged combat is about creating a **rhythm**, and the **Three As** control it: **Action, Aiming and Ammo.**

- **Action:** how firing feels: speed, recoil, sound.
- **Aiming:** free aim, lock-on or auto-aim.
- **Ammo:** how much you carry and how often you reload.
Level design and the health system shape the rhythm too.
A slow, powerful sniper rifle and a fast machine gun create completely different rhythms, even with the same controls.
On mobile, aiming is the hardest A, so most shooters add auto-fire, auto-aim or aim help. Be generous with ammo: running dry with no backup makes players quit.
Action, Aiming, Ammo: load it, point it, feed it.

check.q: What are the Three As of ranged combat?
options: Action, Aiming, Ammo
Attack, Armour, Agility
Aim, Alert, Assist
check.why: Together they set the rhythm of shooting.

cards.text: Start from **real-world weapon roles**, then make every weapon **useful and different.** Each gets a clear job, and any overlap comes with a trade-off.
A shotgun is strong up close and weak far away. A sniper rifle is the opposite. A machine gun is fast but less accurate. Clear strengths and weaknesses make choices interesting.
Never leave the player holding an empty gun with no backup, like a knife. Feeling powerless makes players quit.
In hero shooters and card games, each unit fills one role: tank, damage dealer, healer or controller. If two units do the same job, one is a clone wearing a fake moustache.
One gun, one job.

check.q: Two weapons do exactly the same job. What's wrong?
options: One is redundant and adds no real choice
Nothing: more weapons are always better
They just need more different colours
check.why: Each weapon should have its own niche or a clear trade-off.

cards.text: Many shooting moments take movement away from the player: shooting galleries, mounted guns, vehicles and rails. Then the work is **readability, fair target timing and spectacle.**
When the game controls movement, targets must appear where the player can see them, with enough time to react. Scripted moments become the show.
A rail shooter is like a haunted house ride where you're allowed to shoot back.
Many mobile shooters and playable ads are rail-style: the game moves you, you just tap targets. Perfect for one thumb and short sessions.

check.q: In a rail shooter, what must the designer get right?
options: Targets that appear clearly, with time to react
Free movement controls in every direction
Long reload times to add more tension
check.why: When players can't move, fairness depends on target placement and timing.

cards.text: **Variety is fun.** Grenades, smart bombs, fire and poison each need clear warning, feedback and limits. If you take control away from the player, do it carefully, and **always leave a way to fight back.**

Disabling attacks: stun, knockback, knockdown, grabbing on, transforming, losing balance, sliding. Prefer disabling over instant killing. Poison should be rare, with a common antidote, and never hopeless.
A **smart bomb** clears the whole screen. It's a great relief valve when the player is overwhelmed, but it must be limited, or it makes every fight trivial.
Genshin Impact turns fire and other elements into a whole system: combine two elements for a reaction. Show weaknesses with icons before the fight, and never sell the only counter.
Rare poison, common antidote, never hopeless.

check.q: What must every disabling attack leave the player?
options: A way to fight back or escape
Nothing: that's the point
A shop offer
check.why: Total helplessness feels unfair and makes players quit.

lessons.title: Health: how much and how to show it

cards.text: Combat only matters if the player has **something to lose.** Size health with simple maths, **show it so it can't be missed**, and pick a way to regain it that fits your pace.

Rogers' formula: **starting health = number of hits the player should survive × average damage per hit.** For example, 20 hits × 10 damage = 200 health. Then regain it by pickups, by resting, or slowly over time.
In GTA, a damaged car drags its bumper and smokes. You don't need a health bar to know it's about to explode.
Show health above every unit in mobile action games, in team colours. Players glance for less than a second, so health must read instantly.
Hits × Hurt = Health.

check.q: Players should survive 20 hits of 10 damage. What starting health?

lessons.title: Death is a door, not a wall

cards.text: Lives and game-over screens came from **arcades selling coin plays.** In a game the player already owns, death should **teach and motivate**, never waste time or punish twice.

Good death design:
- the player sees clearly why they died
- restarting is fast and close by
- no long walk back or repeated cutscene
- a reason to try once more
Arcade death sold coins. Good modern death sells "one more try".
F2P death often sells continues: "+5 moves" or "revive". That's fine after a real mistake. It turns predatory when levels are tuned so you almost always need one.
Death is a door, not a wall.

check.q: What should a good death screen do?
options: Show why you died and get you back fast
Play a long, dramatic death animation
Send you back to the start of the level
check.why: Death should teach and motivate, not waste time.

lessons.title: F2P combat: where does the skill live?

cards.text: Taken to the extreme, "Batman never misses" becomes **auto-battle**: the game fights, and **you decide** the team, the timing and the upgrades. The question is **where the skill lives.**

- **Full action** (Brawl Stars, Genshin Impact): skill is in aiming, dodging and timing.
- **Turn-based with auto** (Honkai: Star Rail): skill is in team building.
- **Auto with ultimates you trigger:** skill is in timing the big attack.
- **Idle** (AFK Arena): skill is in the roster.
Counter systems make choices matter: Pokémon GO's type chart, Raid: Shadow Legends' affinity triangle, Clash Royale's air vs ground cards. Show them with clear icons before the fight.
Always offer a counter players can get by playing. If the only answer to a common threat is a paid hero, it's pay-to-win.
Auto plays the fight; you play the matchup.

check.q: In an idle auto-battler, where does the player's skill mostly live?
options: Choosing and building the team
Aiming shots at the right moment
Dodging attacks with quick swipes
check.why: When fights run themselves, the decisions move to the roster.
